a computational theory in which layer 2/3 (L2/3) integrates past sensory input, relayed via layer 4, with top-down context to predict incoming sensory stimuli. Learning is self-supervised by comparing L2/3 predictions with the latent representations of actual sensory input arriving at L5 6 This recent study illustrates fig. 1 Information flow in neocortical circuits (Figure). This recent study illustrates fig. 2 A model of temporal self-supervised learning in cortical circuits (Figure).

What is the cognitive lightcone of a cortical column, each cortical layer, and each cortical neuron (remind the reader of how complex a cortical pyramidal neuron is) from a representational view (give examples)? spatial and temporal receptive fields across the hierarchy

Relying heavily on George 2025 since their model is consistent with the overarching frameworks of Bayesian inference, predictive coding, and free energy minimization, all while being validated on real-world tasks and accounting for several visual phenomena seen in humans. Will cover Numenta’s work too.

 80% of total brain volume but only 16-20% of total brain neurons (in humans)

Shaped like a crumpled napkin laid on top of the brain

Evolutionarily

Neocortex is a mammalian innovation ( 200 million years ago)

Six-layered structure is highly conserved across mammals

Represents elaboration of simpler 3-layered reptilian cortex

Expansion rather than new invention drove primate/human brain evolution

Columns and Minicolumns

Basic structural unit: minicolumns containing 80-120 neurons,  28-40 μm diameter 7

Maintain consistent 28-40 μm diameters with 50 μm spacing, creating a remarkably uniform grid across the cortical surface

"Receive common inputs, have common outputs, are interconnected" - putative fundamental computational unit

Developmental basis: Rakic’s Radial Unit Hypothesis - radial glial progenitors produce clonal pyramidal neurons migrating into layers

Contains all major cortical cell phenotypes interconnected vertically

Controversy over functional significance

Originally: discrete structures with cells responsive to single modality 8

Critics: no evidence for discrete structural entities, no canonical circuit demonstrated 9

Term evolved to encompass diverse vertical organizations (functional columns, hypercolumns, OD columns, barrels)

Computational perspective from Bio-RCN 10

Column = binary random variable representing feature/concept (oriented line in V1, letter in IT)

Different laminae compute feature’s participation in various contexts:

Lateral: with other features at same level

Hierarchical: with parent/child features

Pooling: for invariant representations

Vertical connections genetically specified; lateral connections learned through experience

Layerwise Functions

Layer 1: Feedback integration hub

No excitatory somata, only GABAergic interneurons 11

Receives long-range feedback projections that extend horizontally

Pyramidal neurons from other layers access top-down context via apical dendrites

Unique 5HT3aR-expressing interneurons specialized for this layer

Layer 2/3: Lateral connectivity and pooling

Implements contour continuity and feature association [Bio-RCN]

Long-range patchy connections spanning columns (up to 500-1000 μm)

Complex cells perform pooling for transformation invariance

Feed-forward output to higher cortical areas

Learned lateral connections (not genetically specified)

Layer 4: Primary feed-forward processing

Spiny stellate cells receive thalamic input

Computes feature likelihood from bottom-up evidence [Bio-RCN]

Projects primarily to layers 2/3 and 5 within column

Absent in motor areas ("agranular cortex")

Layer 5: Belief integration and output

Combines feed-forward and feedback to compute feature "beliefs" [Bio-RCN]

Largest pyramidal cells (Betz cells in motor cortex)

Major subcortical projections (striatum, brainstem, spinal cord)

Two subpopulations: 5a (cortical projections) vs 5b (subcortical)

Implements lateral propagation with top-down modulation

Projects to thalamus, where local features are reconciled with global cortical states

Layer 6: Feedback to lower hierarchical levels

Unpacks feature beliefs into component messages [Bio-RCN]

Projects to thalamus (completing cortico-thalamic loops)

Modulates incoming sensory information via thalamic feedback

Multiple subpopulations with distinct projection patterns

Thalamus has been informally referred to as "layer 7 of the cortex"

Information Flow Patterns

Three canonical streams:

Feed-forward: L4 -> L2/3 -> L5 within area; L2/3 -> L4 between areas

Feedback: L5/6 -> L1 (and other layers) of lower areas

Lateral: L2/3 <-> L2/3 between areas at same hierarchical level

Implements hierarchical Bayesian inference [Bio-RCN]

Forward pass: evidence accumulation and feature detection

Backward pass: context and predictions from higher levels

Lateral pass: ensures consistency across spatial/feature dimensions

Electrophysiology reveals a conserved "spectrolaminar" motif–gamma oscillations peaking in superficial layers and alpha-beta rhythms in deep layers-across macaque, marmoset and human, hinting that columnar modules share a common frequency-division multiplexing scheme for feed-forward, feedback and lateral messages A circuit model illustrates one possible implementation of laminar computations (Figure) 72. The proposed network produces oscillatory activity (Figure).

Flexibility within stereotypy

Basic laminar plan genetically specified

Vertical intracolumnar connections developmentally determined

Lateral intercolumnar connections learned through experience

Allows adaptation to environmental statistics while maintaining computational architecture

Functional Specializations by Area

Cellular specializations

Determined by sensory modality/modalities being fed in (ferret study)

Chart out where each modality lands

Primary sensory: prominent L4, clear laminar segregation

Motor cortex: absent L4, large L5 pyramidal cells

Association areas: less distinct lamination, more complex connectivity

Species/area-specific variations in columnar organization

Not all mammals show clear columns (less evident in rodents)

Column width varies: 350-600 μm for macrocolumns

Primate V1:  2.5x more neurons per minicolumn than other areas

Thousand Brains Theory and Monty

Semi-independence of cortical columns

Grid cells in every cortical column; dedicated grid cell layer

"Seemingly all" cortical columns having motor outputs

Cortical columns vote laterally across the hierarchy and receive contextual information from higher levels

Cover Monty in depth

The thalamus

What is the learning rule? What is it optimizing?

Has been called the seventh layer of the cortex by Numenta

Acts as a nexus between sensory inputs, cortex, and subcortex

’Core’ thalamic nuclei route precise sensory/motor content to specific primary cortical layers, while ’matrix’ (higher-order) nuclei project diffusely to superficial cortex to coordinate widespread activity

Thalamic gating mechanisms provide temporal coordination across distributed cortical networks, enabling synchronized processing of multimodal sensory information and top-down predictions from higher-order areas

Higher-order thalamic nuclei (pulvinar, mediodorsal, etc.) act as dynamic switchboards, routing context-dependent information between cortical areas and synchronizing their rhythms to support cortical cooperation and flexibility.

For instance, the pulvinar nucleus (greatly expanded in primates) interconnects visual cortical areas in parallel loops, implementing attention by modulating gain and synchrony

Anatomically, every major cortico-cortical pathway tends to have a parallel cortico-pulvinar-cortical route ("replication principle"), which allows the thalamus to adjust the precision of inter-area signals and bind distributed cortical representations. In effect, cortico-thalamo-cortical loops enable iterative processing: cortical predictions drive thalamic neurons and thalamus feeds back integrative signals to cortex, essential for sensory gating, attention, and evidence accumulation

Overall, thalamus can be though of as a global cortical coherence operator; think of it like a distributed system coordinator - while each node (cortical area) handles its specialized computation, the thalamus ensures the overall system reaches coherent, globally consistent solutions.

More in "Loops" section

Brief Recap of Cortical Architecture

The cortical column–a vertically organized ensemble spanning roughly 300–600μm300–600\mu m in diameter and all six cortical layers–has long been proposed as the fundamental repeating computational unit of cortex 12, 13. Though the degree of columnar discreteness varies across areas and species–and the concept remains debated 14, 15–there is broad agreement that the laminar microcircuit constitutes a canonical motif that is replicated, with quantitative variations in cell density, layer thickness, and connectivity ratios, across nearly all cortical areas 16, 3, 17.

For the purposes of understanding cortical learning, the key architectural features of this microcircuit are the following (readers should refer to the "Whole-Brain Architecture and Information Flow" section for full anatomical detail):

1. Laminar segregation of signal types. Thalamic and lower-area feedforward input arrives predominantly in the granular layer (L4), where it is relayed upward to superficial layers (L2/3). Feedback projections from higher areas target preferentially the superficial layers (especially L1) and deep layers (L5/6), largely bypassing L4 18, 19, 20, 17. This laminar separation means that, at each stage of the hierarchy, bottom-up data and top-down contextual or predictive signals are anatomically segregated before being integrated–a structural prerequisite exploited by nearly every computational theory of cortical learning, from predictive coding 21, 22 to biased competition 23. Layer 1 in particular functions as an integration and control plane: it is a major termination zone for long-range feedback and higher-order thalamic input onto apical tufts, and it is densely innervated by neuromodulatory fibers and specialized inhibitory circuits that gate whether top-down signals actually influence somatic output and plasticity 24.

2. Excitatory recurrence dominates. The majority of excitatory synapses onto a cortical pyramidal neuron originate from other cortical pyramidal neurons within the same area or from feedback projections, rather than from feedforward thalamic or lower-area inputs 25, 26, 27. The cortex is thus predominantly a recurrent prediction machine rather than a feedforward feature-extraction pipeline. This architectural fact has profound implications for learning: the majority of synaptic weights that must be tuned are those mediating lateral and top-down recurrent dynamics, and the dominant "input" to any given neuron is the cortex’s own ongoing internal model, not the external world directly. Moreover, synaptic efficacies (and their spine-size correlates) in cortex are heavy-tailed and well-described by log-normal-like distributions, implying that cortical computation/learning is often dominated by a minority of strong synapses embedded in a sea of weak ones 28, 29. A 2026 model examines distributed predictive processing (Figure) 73. A data-constrained model tests distributed prediction (Figure).

3. Feedback connections vastly outnumber feedforward (but are often weaker per pathway). Quantitative tract-tracing shows that feedback projections are typically more numerous and more diffuse than feedforward projections, both in the number of source areas and in the fraction of labeled neurons per connection 30, 31. However, detailed analyses of laminar connection rules suggest a complementary nuance: feedforward pathways tend to have higher weights, cross fewer hierarchical levels, and are less numerous than feedback pathways, and the hierarchy is constructed from supra- and infragranular counterstreams in which both bottom-up and top-down signals can be point-to-point in supragranular layers while infragranular streams are more diffuse 20. This asymmetry remains exactly what one would expect of a predictive hierarchy: rich high-dimensional expectations must be broadcast downward and compared locally against sparser ascending data streams. This anatomical counterstream organization has a physiological correlate: in human visual cortex, directed inter-areal influences consistent with feedforward signaling are strongest in the gamma band, whereas feedback influences are strongest in the alpha–beta range, supporting the idea that cortex can multiplex predictions and prediction-error–like traffic in distinct spectral channels 32, 33.

4. The pyramidal neuron as a multi-compartment learning unit. The principal excitatory neuron of the cortex–the pyramidal cell–is far more than a simple integrate-and-fire point neuron. Its elaborate dendritic arbor is functionally compartmentalized into at least two semi-independent integration zones: the basal/proximal dendrites, which primarily receive feedforward and local recurrent input, and the apical tuft dendrites in layer 1, which receive feedback, contextual, and modulatory input from higher areas and nonspecific thalamic nuclei 34, 35. When sufficiently strong basal (bottom-up) and apical (top-down) inputs coincide, the neuron can generate dendritic calcium spikes that dramatically boost its firing rate–a coincidence-detection mechanism sometimes called backpropagation-activated calcium spike firing (BAC firing) 35, 36. This architecture means that individual pyramidal neurons can, in principle, use dendritic nonlinearities to implement powerful context-sensitive gating of bottom-up drive by top-down input 37, 38. However, it is often safer to treat apical feedback not as a literal subtractive "error" input but as a contextual/precision signal that can nonlinearly gate which bottom-up patterns win and which synapses are eligible for strengthening; recent causal work shows that cortico-cortical feedback can recruit branch-specific apical dendritic events consistent with nonlinear integration of top-down signals 39.

5. Distinct pyramidal cell classes serve distinct computational roles. Deep-layer pyramidal neurons are not a monolithic population. Layer 5 contains at least two major classes: intratelencephalic (IT) neurons projecting to other cortical areas and striatum, and extratelencephalic (ET, or pyramidal tract) neurons projecting to subcortical targets including thalamus, brainstem, and spinal cord 40, 3, 41. Layer 6 contains corticothalamic (CT) neurons that provide modulatory feedback to thalamic relay nuclei. These distinct output channels mean that the "predictions" and "errors" computed within a column can be routed to qualitatively different targets–subcortical motor systems, thalamic relay and modulatory circuits, other cortical areas–each of which may use the signal differently for its own learning. Recent single-cell transcriptomic and connectomic studies have further revealed that even within these broad classes, there exist finer-grained subtypes with distinct connectivity, gene expression, and likely plasticity profiles 42, 43. Patch-seq reconstructions and voltage traces show the morphological and electrophysiological range of mouse cortical neuron types (Figure) 74. Human supragranular pyramidal neuron types differ visibly in dendritic morphology and intrinsic electrophysiology (Figure) 75.

6. Interneuron diversity enables flexible error computation. Cortical circuits contain a rich repertoire of GABAergic interneuron types–parvalbumin-expressing (PV) basket and chandelier cells, somatostatin-expressing (SST) Martinotti cells, vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing (VIP) interneurons, and others–each of which targets distinct compartments of pyramidal neurons and is embedded in distinct circuit motifs 44, 45. PV interneurons provide powerful perisomatic inhibition that regulates gain and timing; SST interneurons preferentially target apical dendrites, gating top-down input; VIP interneurons predominantly inhibit SST interneurons, creating a disinhibitory motif (VIP->SST->pyramidal) that can selectively "open the gate" for feedback signals when attention or surprise is high 46, 47, 48. For cortical learning, this interneuron diversity is not a complication–it is the machinery through which the cortex flexibly computes, gates, and routes error signals across dendritic compartments, layers, and behavioral states.

7. Thalamocortical and cortico-subcortical loops. Each cortical area is embedded in reciprocal loops with the thalamus–both through "first-order" relay nuclei (receiving ascending sensory input) and "higher-order" nuclei such as the pulvinar and mediodorsal nucleus (receiving cortical layer 5 input and projecting back to cortex), which have been proposed to function as a flexible routing and gain-control substrate for cortico-cortical communication 49, 50. Cortical areas are also embedded in parallel loops through the basal ganglia (via striatal input and thalamic return) and the cerebellum (via pontine nuclei, cerebellar cortex, deep nuclei, and thalamic return) 51, 52. The learning implications are twofold: first, the thalamus is not a passive relay but an active partner in cortical learning, capable of gating plasticity and mediating inter-areal credit assignment; second, the cortex never learns in isolation–its representations are continuously shaped by reinforcement signals from the basal ganglia, predictive error signals from the cerebellum, and memory-replay signals from the hippocampus, as outlined in the introduction to this section.

8. A note on areal variation. While the canonical microcircuit provides a useful common framework, it is important to acknowledge that cortical areas differ quantitatively in ways that affect their learning dynamics. Primary sensory areas have a thick, neuron-dense L4 (granular cortex), reflecting their role as the main recipients of thalamic feedforward input, whereas agranular cortex (e.g., primary motor cortex, anterior cingulate, orbitofrontal cortex) has a diminished or absent L4 and expanded deep layers, reflecting a shift from sensory reception toward output and top-down control 53, 54. Importantly, this granularity gradient correlates with gradients in plasticity: agranular and dysgranular areas in the prefrontal and limbic cortex exhibit markers of higher synaptic turnover and plasticity (e.g., higher expression of growth-associated proteins, lower myelination, and higher spine density turnover), whereas heavily myelinated primary sensory areas show greater synaptic stability after critical-period closure 55, 56. The implication is that the learning rate and plasticity regime of the cortical optimizer are not spatially uniform but are graded along the cortical hierarchy–a theme we return to when discussing cortical learning across development.

9. The Principal Gradient and Hierarchy of Timescales. The cortex is organized along a continuous macroscopic gradient of connectivity and gene expression, stretching from primary sensory/motor regions to transmodal association areas (e.g., the default mode network) 57, 58. This structural gradient imposes a corresponding hierarchy of temporal receptive windows. Lower areas (e.g., V1, A1) possess strong intrinsic inhibition and fast membrane time constants, optimizing them to learn rapid, transient sensory fluctuations. As one ascends the gradient, excitation/inhibition ratios shift and recurrent connection strengths increase, lengthening the intrinsic integration window 59, 60, 61. This forces higher areas to "ignore" high-frequency noise and instead learn slow, invariant, and abstract regularities (e.g., social narratives or long-term goals) 62, 63. Thus, the "optimization horizon" is not uniform; the cortical architecture enforces a spectral decomposition of the learning problem, with different areas theoretically "assigned" to minimize prediction error over different timescales. A 2025 preprint measures neural timescales across the mouse brain (Figure) 76. The preprint maps timescales across brain regions (Figure).

10. Small-World Topology and "Rich Club" Hubs. Beyond the laminar microcircuit, the global connectivity of the cortex exhibits a "small-world" topology: high local clustering (supporting specialized, modular learning) combined with short path lengths (supporting global error propagation) 64, 65. Crucially, this network possesses a "rich club" of densely interconnected high-degree hubs (e.g., precuneus, superior frontal cortex, insula) that serve as a high-capacity backbone for integrating information across modules 66, 67. For an optimization system, this topology represents a trade-off between segregation and integration: local modules can update their weights to minimize local prediction errors without causing catastrophic interference elsewhere, while the rich club provides a high-capacity backbone for rapid global coordination when model updates must be system-wide 68, 69.

11. Topographic interfaces. Many cortical and cortico-subcortical projections preserve topography (retinotopy, tonotopy, somatotopy, and related continuous maps), which constrains learning by making prediction errors spatially local and credit assignment more tractable: nearby units share receptive fields and can update coherently without global rewiring 70. Topographic precision is also cell-type- and area-dependent in major learning loops (e.g., corticostriatal projections), implying that what the basal ganglia can reinforce is constrained by the geometric alignment between cortical representational space and striatal input channels 71.

In sum, the cortical architecture reviewed here–laminar segregation of feedforward and feedback signals, massive recurrence, feedback-dominated connectivity, multi-compartment pyramidal neurons, diverse inhibitory interneuron types, embedding in thalamocortical and cortico-subcortical loops, and genetically-specified macroscopic cortico-cortico connectivity motifs–is not merely a substrate on which learning happens. It is an architecture designed for a particular kind of learning: the continuous, hierarchical comparison of internally generated predictions with externally and internally driven signals, and the use of resulting mismatches to refine a deep generative model of the world. The sections that follow examine how this architecture realizes each step of the optimization loop–what the cortex is optimizing, how errors are computed and propagated, how credit is assigned, and what plasticity mechanisms implement the resulting weight updates.

See "The Cortex" in the "Optimization Architecture" section.
